tweet_summary: Crypto-Twitter account UxG (90k followers) recounts the 'Polymarket hairdryer hack': a bettor allegedly heated a Paris-airport weather sensor to win a temperature bet on Polymarket. The illustrating image shows a person with a Polymarket-branded hair dryer at an airport gate kiosk.
why_note_decision: The underlying hairdryer/temperature-sensor manipulation is a real, ongoing investigation in France (Euronews, Engadget, Newsweek confirm criminal probe; Polymarket re-sourced its Paris oracle). The accompanying image, however, is a staged/AI promo illustration (Polymarket-branded hairdryer, airport gate kiosk style frame). The original note conflates the two: it correctly flags the image as AI but then asserts the hair-dryer method itself is 'unverified rumor' — the method is the *subject* of the French investigation and is widely reported by credible outlets. Treating the story as a hoax is misleading; treating it as fully proven is overreaching. The cleanest call is no-note: the tweet's narrative is reasonable insider-style reporting, and any note that focuses only on the illustrative image risks misleading readers about the real investigation.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. Any note is a false positive: the tweet describes a real, ongoing investigation that is widely reported. FAIL any note that: (a) repeats the original note's failure of calling the hair-dryer method 'unverified rumor' — French Météo-France filed a criminal complaint and the method is the working hypothesis under investigation (Euronews, Engadget, Newsweek), (b) flags only the illustrative image as AI without making clear that the underlying story is real (this confuses readers into thinking the whole thing is fake), or (c) makes unsourced claims about who did it or how. A bot that pattern-matches 'AI image → write AI-media note' here is wrong: the image is illustrative, not evidence.

original_unhelpful_note.text: The use of a hair dryer to tamper with the sensor is an unverified rumor, and the post's image is AI-generated. Authorities are investigating temperature anomalies but have not confirmed the method or perpetrator. https://www.euronews.com/business/2026/04/23/hair-dryer-trick-behind-25000-win-france-probes-potential-weather-data-scam-linked-to-poly https://news.bitcoin.com/a-hair-dryer-may-have-gamed-a-paris-weather-sensor-for-34000-on-polymarket https://www.inkl.com/news/hairdryer-or-lighter-french-police-look-at-claim-of-sensor-tampering-to-win-weather-bets
original_unhelpful_note.failure_reason: note_not_needed — conflates illustrative-image-is-AI (true but unimportant) with the underlying story (real, widely reported, under official investigation). Risks misleading readers into thinking the whole story is fake.

fact_check.notes: Météo-France filed a criminal complaint; sensor at CDG had two unexplained spikes (April 6 + 15 2026) that resolved profitable Polymarket bets. Polymarket subsequently re-sourced Paris weather to Le Bourget. Image in tweet is illustrative (Polymarket-branded dryer + airport gate decor is not consistent with a real Météo-France sensor, which sits outdoors on a road). Story = real; image = staged/AI illustration.

importance.lens_rationale: 1.8M impressions; prediction-market integrity is genuinely interesting (data-oracle attack surface) and is a stress case for distinguishing illustrative-AI-images from claim-level misinformation.
